newsitem.title: ISRAEL: World Bank economist blasts Israel's Netanyahu.
newsitem.headline: World Bank economist blasts Israel's Netanyahu.

text.p: World Bank chief economist Michael Bruno blasted Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday for a lack of "serious thinking" on economic reforms.

Bruno, asked by Israel radio to review Netanyahu's economic performance after nearly six months in office, praised the prime minister's rhetoric on budget cuts and economic liberalisation but said Israel needed action, not talk.
"What stands out in the economy in these 180 days...is that there is talk, talk, and more talk but nothing is being done," Bruno told the radio.
"The most worrying thing is the double messages we are hearing from the prime minister's office," he said.
Bruno, who was Bank of Israel governor from 1986 to 1991, attacked Netanyahu for not following through on repeated calls for capital market reforms and broad economic liberalisation.

He said Netanyahu's proposals to cut government spending by some seven billion shekels in 1997 to narrow a soaring budget deficit were incompatible with his calls for increased defence spending and promises to coalition partners.
"The talk about raising the defence budget...is simply contradictory. So are the promises he has made to various parties saying 'I won't cut this, I'll find another way.'
"These are all double messages giving the impression that this thing is unplanned and there has not been serious thinking until the end," Bruno said.
Netanyahu this week called for stepped up defence spending in light of tensions with Israel's Arab neighbours which have re-ignited since the right-winger took office in June.
The proposed budget cuts fall mainly on housing and social welfare spending. Members of the prime minister's own coalition have vowed to fight the cuts which they say target the poor.
"In the Israeli economy, you can't make serious budget cuts only in welfare without making them in defence," Bruno said.

Bruno said he was concerned Netanyahu's tough stance on Middle East peace moves could jeopardise the increased foreign investment and access to new markets created by the previous government's peace deals with the Palestinians and Jordan.

"There is one very good legacy left by the former government and that is the peace process, which had a positive projection in the economic realm. I have a serious suspicion from what I see and hear that this legacy could be spoiled," he said.
Bruno urged Netanyahu to move decisively on his proposals.

"Budget cuts will allow changes in the exchange rate. It will allow the Bank of Israel governor to lower interest rates. It will allow visible growth in exports. It will allow a fall in long-range interest rates," he said.
"Only he (Netanyahu) can take a decision like this."
